query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A tailored phase‐selective recrystallization heat treatment applied to as‐cast eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) will simultaneously increase both their strength and ductility by refining the strain partitioning between the soft (fcc) and hard (B2) phases, mediated through the formation of a fully recrystallized, ductile soft phase embedded in a continuous hard-phase framework.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine dual-phase (lamellar fcc + B2) microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled phase-selective recrystallization heat treatment that fully recrystallizes the soft fcc phase while retaining a continuous hard B2 phase framework.
generation.conditions: The treatment should be performed at temperatures and times chosen such that only the fcc phase recrystallizes (e.g., via a two-step thermo-mechanical schedule) with tests conducted at room temperature under quasi-static loading conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A microstructure where a fully recrystallized, ductile soft phase is embedded within a skeleton of a hard phase, leading to improved strain partitioning and reduced weak interphase boundaries.
generation.mechanism: By selectively recrystallizing only the soft phase, the process minimizes flaws at phase interfaces and leverages the inherent strain hardening of both phases. The hard phase provides a load-bearing skeleton while the soft phase’s refined structure enables uniform deformation, delaying crack initiation and favoring simultaneous enhancement of strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy is expected to exhibit higher ultimate tensile strength (around or above ~2 GPa) along with a substantial increase in uniform elongation (potentially reaching ~35%), relative to the as-cast baseline which typically has lower strain hardening and ductility.
generation.baseline: As-cast eutectic HEA exhibiting a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure with typical strength and ductility values lower than those achieved after phase-selective recrystallization.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the intervention may be sensitive to exact heat treatment parameters, alloy composition variations, and phase volume fractions; outside an optimal processing window the intervention may not improve both properties concurrently.
generation.uncertainty: While previous reports indicate enhanced ductility via phase-selective recrystallization in similar EHEA systems, quantitative improvements in strength and ductility may vary with processing conditions. The optimal thermal parameters and the scalability of the process for different alloy compositions remain to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical as-cast eutectic HEA samples. Subject one set to the proposed phase-selective recrystallization heat treatment while keeping the other set as-cast (or using a non-selective annealing treatment). Perform systematic quasi-static tensile tests on both sets.
measurements: Tensile stress-strain curves (to extract ultimate tensile strength, yield strength, and uniform elongation)
Microstructural characterization (via SEM/EBSD/TEM) to verify selective recrystallization of the soft phase and integrity of the hard phase skeleton
Fractography to assess crack initiation sites and interface quality
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat treatment does not produce a microstructure with a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded within a continuous hard phase, or if the treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant simultaneous increase in both strength and ductility (relative to the baseline), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Excellent ductility is crucial not only for shaping but also for strengthening metals and alloys. The ever most widely used eutectic alloys are suffering from the limited ductility and losing competitiveness among advanced structural materials. Here we report a distinctive concept of phase-selective recrystallization to overcome this challenge for eutectic alloys by triggering the strain hardening capacity of the duplex phases completely. We manipulate the strain partitioning behavior of the two phases in a eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) to obtain the phase-selectively recrystallized microstructure with a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded in the skeleton of a hard phase. The resulting microstructure fully releases the strain hardening capacity in EHEA by eliminating the weak boundaries. Our phase-selectively recrystallized EHEA achieves a high ductility of ∼35% uniform elongation with true stress of ∼2 GPa. This concept is universal for various duplex alloys with soft and hard phases and opens new frontiers for traditional eutectic alloys as high-strength metallic materials. Eutectic alloys have achieved a dominant position in the history of human civilization,, e.g., cast irons in agricultural society, casting aluminum alloys in modern industry, and eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) in advanced metallic materials. Excellent castability, free of segregations/defects, and self-generated dual phases make eutectic alloys significantly advantaged in low-cost mass-production and balanced strength-ductility combination,. However, these advantages are fading away with the rapid development of advanced structural materials due to the unsatisfactory deformability of eutectic alloys and limited metallurgical mechanisms to ductilize them. The cracking of weak interfaces, including phase boundaries (PBs) and grain boundaries (GBs) of the hard phases, causes premature failure during the uniaxial tension of eutectic alloys,. This situation results in the low tensile elongation of eutectic alloys even though their phases are both strain hardenable intrinsically.
